turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that his actions were not a threat, but a statement of fact, and that he had been documenting the instances of oppression against his tenantry, and would not hesitate to take further action if necessary.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil if his documentation of the instances of oppression would be made public.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Bimala that as long as the records were not made public, the oppressors would think they had impunity, and that he needed her understanding on this matter.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil if he had considered the consequences of involving outsiders in the affairs of the estate.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that Bimala understood the gravity of the situation and the need for him to take decisive action to protect their tenantry.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil what measures he had taken to protect the tenantry from potential attacks, and how the estate's interests would be safeguarded in such a scenario.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that the situation was not to be taken lightly and that he would not be swayed by petty sarcasm.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was still collecting his rent from the Mussulmans while threatening to protect the tenantry, or had his priorities suddenly shifted.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil said to Sandip that his actions were guided by a sense of duty to the estate and its people, and that he would not be swayed by personal considerations.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that his concern for the estate's interests was admirable, but he was beginning to sound like a broken record, and it was time for some new melodies to be sung.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that his flippant attitude was a disservice to the very people he was supposed to protect.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip said that Nikhil's warnings were as tedious as a rainy day in Bengal, and that he would rather listen to a recitation of the Mahabharata than hear another word about Mussulman attacks.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil if his concerns about the Mussulman attacks were based on specific information or mere speculation.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that the threat of Mussulman attacks was not mere speculation, but based on concrete evidence from reliable sources.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip said that Nikhil's evidence was probably as reliable as a snake oil salesman's claims, and that he'd rather trust his own instincts than Nikhil's so-called 'concrete evidence'.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Sandip if he had considered the possibility that the Mussulman attacks might be a symptom of deeper social and economic issues.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that the zamindars of this region had a duty to protect their lands and people from external threats, and that his warnings were not to be taken lightly.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that he was more concerned about Nikhil's lack of vision for the future of their lands than the imaginary threats from the Mussulmans.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil firmly stated that he would not be swayed by Sandip's dismissive attitude, and that the zamindars of this region were accountable for the safety and security of their people.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip retorted that Nikhil was more concerned about preserving his own power and influence than about the welfare of their people.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Bimala where she would go, addressing her as the Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he kept Browning among his books, reminding him of a contest they had over translating lines from Browning, and inquiring if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil and Bimala that he had managed to translate the lines into Bengali, but the result was unlikely to be well-received, and that he had once thought he was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened to prevent it, and he recalled old Dakshina's poetry.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Bimala that it was pointless to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil no longer read poetry since his marriage, but that he, Sandip, was about to be afflicted with the 'fever fit of poesy' again.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that he had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was warning him about the 'fever fit of poesy'.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that for some time, Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were angry with Sandip and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise him to flee.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had come to give him information, not advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil that if the estates were his, a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, and that Nikhil should intimidate the preachers instead of frightening him, and that Nikhil's weakness was also affecting his neighbouring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had not offered him advice, and that he wished Sandip would refrain from giving him his advice, as it was useless, and that there was another thing he wanted to tell Sandip, namely that Sandip and his followers had been secretly oppressing Nikhil's tenantry, and that he could no longer allow that, so he must ask Sandip to leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was threatening him with fear of the Mussulmans, or if there was another fear he had to threaten him with.
